units.title: Transistors as Switches
units.tip: A transistor is an electrically controlled switch that can turn current on or off. MOSFETs are a type of transistor that form the basis of most modern digital chips. Understanding transistors as switches is essential for grasping chip design.

exercises.question: What is a transistor?
exercises.answer: A semiconductor device that acts as an electrically controlled switch
exercises.explain: A transistor uses a control signal (gate voltage) to allow or block current flow between two terminals. This switching behavior is the basis of all digital logic.
choices: A type of resistor that resists electricity
A source of power for the chip
A semiconductor device that acts as an electrically controlled switch

exercises.question: What does MOSFET stand for?
exercises.answer: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
exercises.explain: MOSFET is a type of transistor. The gate (metal) is insulated (oxide) from the silicon channel. A voltage on the gate controls current flow.
choices: Mobile Operating System for Electronic Transistors

exercises.question: What are the three main terminals of a MOSFET?
exercises.answer: Gate, source, and drain
exercises.explain: The gate is the control input. Current flows from drain to source (or source to drain, depending on type). The gate voltage determines whether the transistor is on or off.

exercises.question: What is an NMOS transistor?
exercises.answer: An N-channel MOSFET that conducts when the gate voltage is high
exercises.explain: NMOS transistors turn on (low resistance) when the gate is high (positive voltage). They are used as switches that pull signals to ground.
choices: A transistor that is only used in analog circuits
A transistor that requires no gate voltage
An N-channel MOSFET that conducts when the gate voltage is high
A transistor that always conducts current

exercises.question: What is a PMOS transistor?
exercises.answer: A P-channel MOSFET that conducts when the gate voltage is low
exercises.explain: PMOS transistors turn on (low resistance) when the gate is low (near ground). They are used as switches that pull signals to power supply voltage.
choices: A P-channel MOSFET that conducts when the gate voltage is low
A transistor used only in power supplies
A transistor that always conducts current

exercises.question: When is an NMOS transistor in the ON state?
exercises.answer: When the gate-source voltage exceeds the threshold voltage
exercises.explain: NMOS turns on when the gate voltage rises above the source by more than a threshold, typically a fraction of a volt. The transistor then allows current to flow from drain to source.
choices: When the gate voltage is low
When the gate-source voltage exceeds the threshold voltage
When the drain current is zero

exercises.question: When is a PMOS transistor in the ON state?
exercises.answer: When the gate-source voltage is below the threshold voltage
exercises.explain: PMOS turns on when the gate voltage falls far enough below the source voltage. It allows current to flow from source (at supply voltage) to drain.
choices: When the gate-source voltage is below the threshold voltage
When the drain voltage equals the source voltage
When the gate voltage is high

exercises.question: What is the ON resistance of an ideal transistor?
exercises.answer: Zero, allowing unlimited current flow
exercises.explain: In the ideal ON state, a transistor acts like a closed switch with no resistance. Real transistors have small ON resistance, creating some voltage drop.
choices: The same as the OFF resistance

exercises.question: What is the OFF resistance of an ideal transistor?
exercises.answer: Infinite, blocking all current flow
exercises.explain: In the ideal OFF state, a transistor acts like an open switch with infinite resistance. Real transistors have a small leakage current.
choices: The same as the ON resistance

exercises.question: Why is leakage current a problem in modern chips?
exercises.answer: It wastes power even when transistors are supposed to be off
exercises.explain: As transistors shrink, OFF resistance decreases and leakage increases. This static power consumption limits battery life and generates heat.
choices: It prevents the transistor from turning on
It wastes power even when transistors are supposed to be off

units.title: CMOS Logic Gates
units.tip: CMOS combines NMOS and PMOS transistors to create robust, power-efficient logic gates. Every CMOS gate has a pull-up network (PMOS) and a pull-down network (NMOS).

exercises.question: What is a CMOS inverter?
exercises.answer: One PMOS and one NMOS transistor connected to invert the input
exercises.explain: A CMOS inverter has a PMOS pull-up transistor and an NMOS pull-down transistor in series. When input is high, NMOS pulls output low; when input is low, PMOS pulls it high.
choices: One PMOS and one NMOS transistor connected to invert the input
A logic gate that never switches

exercises.question: In a CMOS inverter, what happens when the input goes high?
exercises.answer: NMOS turns on, pulling output to ground (low)
exercises.explain: When input is high, NMOS conducts, creating a low-resistance path to ground. Simultaneously, PMOS turns off. Output becomes low (0).
choices: PMOS turns on, pulling output to supply voltage
Output stays at the same level
NMOS turns on, pulling output to ground (low)

exercises.question: In a CMOS inverter, what happens when the input goes low?
exercises.answer: PMOS turns on, pulling output to supply voltage (high)
exercises.explain: When input is low, PMOS conducts, creating a low-resistance path to the supply. Simultaneously, NMOS turns off. Output becomes high (1).
choices: NMOS turns on, pulling output to ground
PMOS turns on, pulling output to supply voltage (high)

exercises.question: What is a NAND gate?
exercises.answer: A logic gate that outputs low only when all inputs are high
exercises.explain: NAND (NOT AND) is the complement of AND. It outputs low when all inputs are high, and high otherwise. NAND gates are universal (can build any logic from NAND only).
choices: A gate that requires no transistors
A gate that always outputs the same as the input
A logic gate that outputs low only when all inputs are high

exercises.question: What is a NOR gate?
exercises.answer: A gate that outputs high only when all inputs are low
exercises.explain: NOR (NOT OR) is the complement of OR. It outputs high only when all inputs are low. NOR is also universal for logic synthesis.
choices: A gate that outputs high only when all inputs are low
A gate that outputs high when any input is high

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of CMOS logic?
exercises.answer: Low power consumption because one transistor is always off
exercises.explain: In CMOS, only one of the two series transistors conducts at a time. This eliminates the direct path from supply to ground, reducing static (standby) power.
choices: It works without a power supply
Low power consumption because one transistor is always off
It is faster than all other logic families

exercises.question: What is static power in CMOS?
exercises.answer: Power consumed when the circuit is idle, due to leakage current
exercises.explain: Static power is the baseline power used even when the chip is not switching. It is due to leakage through off transistors. It increases as transistors shrink.
choices: Power consumed when the circuit is idle, due to leakage current

exercises.question: What is dynamic power in CMOS?
exercises.answer: Power consumed when transistors switch, charging and discharging capacitances
exercises.explain: Dynamic power comes from switching activity. Every time a gate switches, capacitors charge and discharge, consuming power proportional to frequency and voltage squared.
choices: Power consumed when transistors switch, charging and discharging capacitances
Power that is independent of frequency
Power consumed only by pull-up transistors

exercises.question: How does CMOS noise margin compare to other logic families?
exercises.answer: CMOS has large noise margins, making it robust to signal degradation
exercises.explain: CMOS logic swings from ground to supply voltage, using the full range. This large swing makes CMOS robust against noise compared to other families.
choices: Noise margins are the same for all logic families
CMOS has very small noise margins
CMOS has large noise margins, making it robust to signal degradation

exercises.question: Why is the ratio of PMOS to NMOS transistor sizes important in CMOS gates?
exercises.answer: To balance the pull-up and pull-down speeds and ensure symmetric switching
exercises.explain: PMOS transistors are inherently slower than NMOS (lower mobility). PMOS must be larger to match NMOS speed. Incorrect sizing causes asymmetric delays.
choices: To reduce the number of transistors
To balance the pull-up and pull-down speeds and ensure symmetric switching

units.title: Standard Cells and Libraries
units.tip: Standard cells are pre-designed, pre-characterized logic gates. A standard cell library contains basic gates, flip-flops, and other building blocks. Chip designers mostly use these cells as components instead of designing transistors from scratch.

exercises.question: What is a standard cell?
exercises.answer: A pre-designed, pre-verified logic gate ready for use in chip designs
exercises.explain: Standard cells (inverter, NAND, NOR, flip-flop, etc.) are library components. They have known timing, power, and area characteristics. Designers build chips by placing and connecting cells.
choices: A pre-designed, pre-verified logic gate ready for use in chip designs
A transistor that is not designed yet

exercises.question: What is in a standard cell library?
exercises.answer: A collection of pre-designed gates, flip-flops, and other logic components
exercises.explain: A cell library includes basic gates (AND, OR, NAND, NOR, inverter), flip-flops, latches, multiplexers, adders, and specialized cells. Each is fully characterized.
choices: A collection of pre-designed gates, flip-flops, and other logic components

exercises.question: What is cell characterization?
exercises.answer: Measuring and documenting timing, power, and area properties of a cell
exercises.explain: Characterization determines how long signals take to propagate through a cell (timing), how much power it consumes, and how much area it occupies.
choices: Designing the transistors inside a cell
Measuring and documenting timing, power, and area properties of a cell

exercises.question: What is a flip-flop cell?
exercises.answer: A standard cell that stores one bit of data, synchronous to a clock
exercises.explain: A flip-flop cell in a standard library is a pre-designed memory element. It is characterized for timing, setup time, hold time, and other parameters.
choices: A standard cell that stores one bit of data, synchronous to a clock
A delay element with no state
A transistor that flips between on and off
A type of logic gate with no memory

exercises.question: Why do chip designers use standard cells instead of designing from transistors?
exercises.answer: Standard cells are pre-verified and pre-characterized, saving time and ensuring quality
exercises.explain: Designing every gate from transistors is error-prone and slow. Standard cells are thoroughly tested and their timing/power is known, so designs are reliable and efficient.
choices: Standard cells are pre-verified and pre-characterized, saving time and ensuring quality
Because transistors cannot be used in modern chips
Because standard cells are always faster

exercises.question: What are different cell library 'variants'?
exercises.answer: Versions of cells optimized for different purposes (speed, area, power)
exercises.explain: A library may provide fast cells (larger, use more power, run quickly), slow cells (smaller, low power, run slowly), and balanced versions for various tradeoffs.
choices: Versions of cells optimized for different purposes (speed, area, power)

exercises.question: What is a 'fast' cell variant?
exercises.answer: A cell with larger transistors that switches quickly but uses more power
exercises.explain: Fast cells have wider transistors for lower resistance and faster switching. They consume more power and area but meet tight timing constraints.
choices: A cell that only works with fast clocks
A cell used only in simulations
A cell with larger transistors that switches quickly but uses more power
A cell that has no delay

exercises.question: What is a 'slow' cell variant?
exercises.answer: A cell with smaller transistors that uses less power but switches slowly
exercises.explain: Slow cells have narrower transistors to save area and power. They have longer delays but are used where timing is not critical.
choices: A cell for low-frequency designs only
A cell that never reaches its output
A cell with smaller transistors that uses less power but switches slowly

exercises.question: What is PVT derating in standard cells?
exercises.answer: Adjusting timing predictions based on process, voltage, and temperature variations
exercises.explain: PVT stands for process, voltage, and temperature. Chips run at different voltages and temperatures and vary from die to die, so PVT derating accounts for how these affect delay and gives designers the worst-case timing.
choices: Adjusting timing predictions based on process, voltage, and temperature variations

exercises.question: Why must timing analysis account for process corners?
exercises.answer: Manufacturing variations cause transistors to behave faster or slower than nominal
exercises.explain: Different chips from the same design vary in speed due to process variations. Fast and slow process corners represent the extremes. Analysis must work at all corners.
choices: Because the factory is located at a corner
Manufacturing variations cause transistors to behave faster or slower than nominal

units.title: The Design Flow
units.tip: Chip design follows a structured flow from high-level description to silicon. RTL (Register Transfer Level) describes the logic. Synthesis converts RTL to gates. Place and route maps gates to physical locations.

exercises.question: What does RTL stand for?
exercises.answer: Register Transfer Level, a description of how data moves between registers
exercises.explain: RTL describes the logic at the register level: what values flow where, on what clock edges, and under what conditions. It is a hardware design abstraction.
choices: Register Transfer Level, a description of how data moves between registers

exercises.question: What is the purpose of the synthesis step?
exercises.answer: Convert RTL into a gate-level netlist of standard cells
exercises.explain: Synthesis reads RTL (usually Verilog) and produces a netlist: a list of standard cells and the nets (wires) connecting them. This is the input to place and route.
choices: Convert RTL into a gate-level netlist of standard cells

exercises.question: What is a netlist?
exercises.answer: A list of cells and nets describing the connections between gates
exercises.explain: A netlist specifies which cells are in the design and how their pins are connected by nets (wires). It is the structured description of the gate-level circuit.
choices: A list of cells and nets describing the connections between gates

exercises.question: What does place and route (PnR) do?
exercises.answer: Assigns cells to physical locations and determines the wiring between them
exercises.explain: PnR takes the netlist and places cells on the chip floorplan, then routes the nets through metal layers. The output is a detailed chip layout.
choices: Assigns cells to physical locations and determines the wiring between them

exercises.question: What is a design constraint?
exercises.answer: A specification (timing, power, area) that the design must satisfy
exercises.explain: Constraints include clock frequency, maximum power, maximum area, pin locations, and timing paths. The design must meet all constraints for signoff.
choices: A transistor that cannot be used
A specification (timing, power, area) that the design must satisfy
A warning message from the tool

exercises.question: What is design verification?
exercises.answer: Testing that the design behaves correctly under all conditions
exercises.explain: Verification includes simulation, formal checking, and other techniques to gain confidence that the design produces correct outputs across the cases that matter.
choices: Testing that the design behaves correctly under all conditions

exercises.question: What is functional verification?
exercises.answer: Verifying that the logic computes the correct outputs
exercises.explain: Functional verification checks that the design produces the right results for the given inputs. It is done via simulation and test vectors.
choices: Verifying that the logic computes the correct outputs

exercises.question: What is design signoff?
exercises.answer: The final approval that all verification and analysis requirements are met
exercises.explain: Signoff means the design is ready for manufacturing. All tests pass, timing is met, power is acceptable, and the layout is correct.
choices: The start of the design process
The final approval that all verification and analysis requirements are met

exercises.question: What is DRC (Design Rule Check)?
exercises.answer: Verification that the layout follows all manufacturing rules
exercises.explain: DRC ensures that metal lines are wide enough, spacing is correct, and all geometric constraints are met so the design can be manufactured.
choices: Verification that the layout follows all manufacturing rules

exercises.question: What is LVS (Layout vs Schematic)?
exercises.answer: Verification that the physical layout matches the circuit schematic
exercises.explain: LVS checks that the layout accurately represents the original circuit. It compares connectivity and ensures no wires were missed or misrouted.
choices: Verification that the physical layout matches the circuit schematic

units.title: Timing and Power
units.tip: Timing analysis ensures the design runs at the required clock frequency without setup or hold violations. Power analysis predicts how much energy the chip will consume, affecting battery life and heat dissipation.

exercises.question: What is static timing analysis (STA)?
exercises.answer: Analysis that computes worst-case delays through the design without simulation
exercises.explain: STA is fast and comprehensive. It calculates signal delays and checks that all timing constraints (setup, hold, clock period) are met. It does not require test vectors.
choices: Analysis that computes worst-case delays through the design without simulation

exercises.question: What is a timing path?
exercises.answer: A sequence of logic gates from an input to an output or register
exercises.explain: A timing path is the chain of combinational logic between two sequential elements (or input to output). Its delay determines whether timing constraints are satisfied.
choices: A sequence of logic gates from an input to an output or register

exercises.question: What is the critical path?
exercises.answer: The timing path with the longest delay, limiting the maximum clock frequency
exercises.explain: The critical path determines the maximum clock frequency. If its delay exceeds the clock period, timing fails. It is the target for optimization.
choices: The shortest path in the design
A path that is never used
The timing path with the longest delay, limiting the maximum clock frequency

exercises.question: What is the setup time of a flip-flop?
exercises.answer: The minimum time the input must be stable before the clock edge
exercises.explain: Setup time is specified by the flip-flop cell. If data changes within this time before the clock edge, the flip-flop may go metastable.
choices: The minimum time the input must be stable before the clock edge
The time to initialize the flip-flop
The duration of the clock pulse

exercises.question: What is setup slack?
exercises.answer: The margin between required time and actual arrival time for a signal
exercises.explain: Positive slack means timing is met with margin. Negative slack indicates a timing violation: the signal arrives too late.
choices: The margin between required time and actual arrival time for a signal

exercises.question: What is the formula for dynamic power?
exercises.answer: P = C * V^2 * F, where C is capacitance, V is voltage, F is frequency
exercises.explain: Dynamic power increases with voltage squared and frequency linearly. Reducing voltage or frequency dramatically cuts dynamic power.
choices: P = C * V^2 * F, where C is capacitance, V is voltage, F is frequency

exercises.question: What is static power?
exercises.answer: Power consumed when the circuit is not switching, due to leakage
exercises.explain: Static power is baseline power from leakage current through off transistors. Leakage rises sharply with temperature and grows with the number of transistors.
choices: Power consumed when the circuit is not switching, due to leakage
Power from the power supply only

exercises.question: How does voltage scaling affect power consumption?
exercises.answer: Lower voltage cuts dynamic power quadratically and also reduces leakage
exercises.explain: Dynamic power scales with V squared, so lowering the supply voltage cuts it sharply. Leakage also falls with lower voltage, which makes voltage scaling a very effective power reduction technique.
choices: Lower voltage cuts dynamic power quadratically and also reduces leakage
Voltage has no effect on power

exercises.question: What is clock gating?
exercises.answer: A technique to disable the clock to inactive parts, saving dynamic power
exercises.explain: Clock gating stops the clock to parts of the chip that are idle, eliminating unnecessary switching and saving dynamic power.
choices: A barrier that blocks the clock
A technique to disable the clock to inactive parts, saving dynamic power
A method to increase clock frequency

exercises.question: What causes power density to be a challenge in modern chips?
exercises.answer: High power consumption in a small area generates excessive heat
exercises.explain: Modern chips pack billions of transistors into small areas. If power consumption is not managed, heat buildup requires expensive cooling and reduces reliability.
choices: The clock frequency is too low
The supply voltage is too low
High power consumption in a small area generates excessive heat

units.title: Fabrication and Packaging
units.tip: Fabrication transforms the chip design into physical silicon on a wafer through photolithography and chemical processing. Packaging protects the die and provides electrical connections to the outside world.

exercises.question: What is a wafer?
exercises.answer: A thin slice of silicon on which many chips are fabricated
exercises.explain: A wafer is a circular silicon disk, commonly 300mm in diameter in modern fabs. Many chips are patterned on each wafer and then separated.
choices: A thin slice of silicon on which many chips are fabricated

exercises.question: What is photolithography?
exercises.answer: The process of using light and photomasks to transfer patterns onto silicon
exercises.explain: Photolithography uses ultraviolet light through a mask to define circuit patterns on photoresist-coated wafers. It repeats for each layer of the chip.
choices: The process of using light and photomasks to transfer patterns onto silicon

exercises.question: What is doping in semiconductor fabrication?
exercises.answer: Adding impurities to silicon to create N-type or P-type regions
exercises.explain: Doping introduces donor atoms (N-type) or acceptor atoms (P-type) into silicon regions to create junctions and transistor channels.
choices: Adding impurities to silicon to create N-type or P-type regions

exercises.question: What is etching in semiconductor fabrication?
exercises.answer: Removing material (silicon, metal, oxide) through chemical or plasma processes
exercises.explain: Etching selectively removes material to create features. Wet etching uses chemicals; dry etching uses plasma. It is precise and repeatable.
choices: Removing material (silicon, metal, oxide) through chemical or plasma processes
Adding new layers to the wafer

exercises.question: What is metallization in chip fabrication?
exercises.answer: Depositing and patterning metal layers to create interconnects
exercises.explain: Metallization deposits metal (usually copper) and patterns it to form wires and connections between transistors. Modern chips have many metal layers.
choices: Depositing and patterning metal layers to create interconnects

exercises.question: What is a die?
exercises.answer: An individual chip cut from the wafer
exercises.explain: A die is one chip unit. After fabrication, the wafer is diced into individual dies. Each die is tested and packaged separately.
choices: An individual chip cut from the wafer

exercises.question: What is chip packaging?
exercises.answer: Mounting the die on a substrate and protecting it with a case
exercises.explain: Packaging protects the silicon die from mechanical damage and environmental hazards. It provides electrical connections through pins or balls to external circuits.
choices: Testing the chip at the factory
Mounting the die on a substrate and protecting it with a case

exercises.question: What is yield in semiconductor manufacturing?
exercises.answer: The percentage of chips on a wafer that pass testing
exercises.explain: Yield is the ratio of working dies to total dies on a wafer. Process defects, contamination, and design issues reduce yield. Low yield increases cost.
choices: The total number of chips manufactured
The percentage of chips on a wafer that pass testing
The speed of the manufacturing process

exercises.question: What are defects in semiconductor manufacturing?
exercises.answer: Physical imperfections (particles, voids, patterns) that cause chips to fail
exercises.explain: Defects include dust particles, voids in metallization, incomplete etching, and pattern imperfections. They cause opens, shorts, or timing failures.
choices: Physical imperfections (particles, voids, patterns) that cause chips to fail

exercises.question: How does chip area affect manufacturing yield?
exercises.answer: Larger chips have lower yield because defects are more likely to hit them
exercises.explain: Yield depends on defect density (defects per unit area). Larger chips expose more area to potential defects, reducing the probability all defects miss the die.
choices: Area has no effect on yield
Larger chips always have higher yield
Larger chips have lower yield because defects are more likely to hit them
